title: Pricing Demo — vertical cut
notes: Standalone piece for LinkedIn and Shorts. Opens with context, not a number.

scenes.narration: This case study grew out of a {#test}real technical assessment for a data analyst role. {#rebuild}I rebuilt the challenge with {#fictional}fictional books and prices, so I could show the process publicly.
scenes.screen: PRICING DEMO / by Alfonso Cifuentes. Real assessment → independent case study, fictional data.

scenes.narration: The task was to analyse a publishing price list. {#trap}The catch? You cannot compare two books fairly until you account for {#attrs}the level, the edition, the format and everything included.
scenes.screen: Two cards that look alike; attributes pull them apart.

scenes.narration: {#six}Six product groups initially looked inconsistent. {#four}Four had a cheaper Starter level. {#two}But two were different: the books had been filed under the wrong series. {#reveal}What looked like pricing problems were actually classification problems.
scenes.screen: Six flags; four Starter; two wrong series; reveal after a pause.

scenes.narration: I left the raw data untouched, corrected the reporting view and reran the comparison. {#result}Consistently priced groups went from [54|fifty-four] {#r56}to [56|fifty-six] out of [60|sixty]. {#web}The interactive case, the fictional dataset and the calculations are on the website. {#sign}I'm Alfonso Cifuentes. This is Pricing Demo.
scenes.screen: 54/60 → 56/60 with the source intact; author and URL.
